```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(easyNIS)
```

## Prepare one survey design

Declare the cohort in `nis_design()` and keep the columns needed by the
summary and model.

```{r design}
nis <- nis_open(nis_example(years = 2019:2020)) |>
  nis_flag_dx(heart_failure = "I50")
design <- nis_design(
  nis,
  cohort = AGE >= 18,
  keep = c(AGE, FEMALE, LOS, DIED, heart_failure),
  annualize = TRUE
)
```

The design contains adult cohort rows. For hospital-years with no cohort rows,
`nis_design()` adds placeholder rows so those hospital-years remain represented
in the design's variance structure. This placeholder method is experimental;
review the design construction and its suitability for your analysis.

## Estimate weighted summaries

`srvyr` adds tidy verbs to survey designs. The total below is an annualized
weighted discharge estimate; the mean and its standard error use the survey
design.

```{r srvyr}
srvyr::summarise(
  design,
  discharges = srvyr::survey_total(),
  mean_age = srvyr::survey_mean(AGE),
  death_rate = srvyr::survey_mean(DIED)
)
```

All values come from invented rows and illustrate output shape only.

## Fit a survey-weighted model

`survey::svyglm()` fits generalized linear models using the design.

```{r model, eval=rlang::is_installed("survey")}
fit <- survey::svyglm(
  DIED ~ heart_failure + AGE + FEMALE + factor(YEAR),
  design = design,
  family = quasibinomial()
)
summary(fit)
```

Coefficients describe model associations under the survey design; they do not
establish causality. The synthetic data are too small and artificial for
substantive conclusions.

## Tables with gtsummary

The examples below use gtsummary 2.6.1 or later.

Pass the result of `nis_design()` directly to `gtsummary::tbl_svysummary()`.
The design supplies cohort discharges for unweighted sample sizes, missing
counts, and category counts. Hospital placeholders contribute to the variance
structure only. This table uses a survey t-test for mean age and the
design-adjusted chi-squared test for sex. The header shows unweighted sample
sizes, alongside weighted summaries in the table body.

```{r table, eval=rlang::is_installed(c("gtsummary (>= 2.6.1)", "cardx", "survey", "gt"))}
gtsummary::tbl_svysummary(
  design,
  by = heart_failure,
  include = c(AGE, FEMALE),
  label = FEMALE ~ "Female",
  statistic = AGE ~ "{mean} ({mean.std.error})",
  missing_stat = "{N_miss_unweighted}"
) |>
  gtsummary::add_p(test = list(AGE ~ "svy.t.test", FEMALE ~ "svy.chisq.test")) |>
  gtsummary::add_overall() |>
  gtsummary::modify_header(gtsummary::all_stat_cols() ~ "**{level}** (unweighted N = {n_unweighted})")
```

Use `tbl_regression()` to format your fitted models and
`tbl_uvregression()` to fit and format a separate survey model for each
predictor. The logistic table reports odds ratios and the linear tables
report differences in mean length of stay.

```{r model-tables, eval=rlang::is_installed(c("gtsummary (>= 2.6.1)", "broom.helpers", "survey", "gt"))}
gtsummary::tbl_regression(fit, exponentiate = TRUE)

los_fit <- survey::svyglm(LOS ~ heart_failure + AGE + FEMALE, design = design)
gtsummary::tbl_regression(los_fit)

gtsummary::tbl_uvregression(
  design,
  y = LOS,
  include = c(heart_failure, AGE, FEMALE),
  method = survey::svyglm
)
```

For Parquet inputs, start with `nis_open()` and then use `nis_design()` to
build the in-memory cohort design used here. Passing a DuckDB-backed survey
`DBIsvydesign` directly to `tbl_svysummary()` fails with gtsummary 2.6.1.
Review unweighted cell counts and apply disclosure rules before sharing.

## Common pitfalls

> **Common pitfalls**
>
> - Use `survey`/`srvyr` methods on the survey design, not ordinary row-level
>   summaries when reporting design-based uncertainty.
> - A weighted estimate does not validate the cohort definition, model, or
>   causal interpretation.
> - Apply disclosure review separately; weighted summaries alone do not show
>   whether counts are safe to report.

See [Survey design and weighting](survey-design.html),
[`nis_design()`](../reference/nis_design.html), and
[Disclosure and suppression](disclosure.html).

## Whole-sample estimation on a laptop

Use `nis_survey()` to estimate means, totals, or regression coefficients when discharge rows would
take too much memory. It uses a nested Taylor design with hospital-year PSUs
and year-specific strata. DuckDB scans the Parquet data and sends weighted
PSU sums to R. Use `dplyr::filter()` on the design to estimate a domain.
`subset(whole, AGE >= 65)` is the survey-style alternative. Filtering the
query before constructing the design changes the sample.

```{r}
whole <- nis_survey(nis)
older <- dplyr::filter(whole, AGE >= 65)
survey::svyby(~LOS, ~YEAR, older, survey::svymean)
fit <- survey::svyglm(LOS ~ AGE + factor(YEAR), older)
broom::tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE)
```

For a `nis_survey()` fit, `gtsummary::tbl_regression()` reports the unweighted
number of complete discharges as N. For a `nis_design()` fit, N comes from
the analysis weights.

Use `nis_design()` for row-level cohort analysis, including quantiles,
chi-square tests, `gtsummary::tbl_svysummary()`, and IPTW. Use the disclosure
workflow before sharing results.
